<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:fpras}
Let $Z\ge0$ be a quantity determined by an input instance. A
\emph{fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme}
($\mathsf{FPRAS}$) for $Z$ is a randomized algorithm that, given the
instance and an accuracy parameter $0<\varepsilon\le1$, returns
$\widehat Z\ge0$ satisfying
\begin{align*}
     \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbf{Pr}\left[(1-\varepsilon) \cdot Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon) \cdot Z\right]}
  {\mathbf{Pr}_{}\left[(1-\varepsilon) \cdot Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon) \cdot Z\right]} &\ge\frac34,
\end{align*}
in time polynomial in the size of the instance and $1/\varepsilon$.\footnote{By the standard median trick, returning the median of $O(\log(1/\delta))$ independent calls boosts the success probability to $1-\delta$ for any $0<\delta<1$.} In the oracle model, each oracle call has unit cost.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:common-bases}
There is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ that, given independence oracles for two matroids ${\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}$ on a common ground set ${\mathcal{U}}$, estimates the number $\left|{{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})\cap{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})}\right|$ of common bases.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The running time of our algorithm is $\widetilde{O}(n^{13}/\varepsilon^{2})$, which certainly isn't optimal. Since our goal is to present our algorithms and proofs in the simplest way possible, we made no attempt to optimize the running time.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:subset-convolution}
Let $\mu,\nu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ be two nonnegative weight functions. We define their \emph{subset convolution} by the quantity
\begin{align*}
    (\mu \ast \nu)(T) &\coloneqq \sum_{S \subseteq T} \mu(S) \cdot \nu(T \setminus S)
             =\left[{\bm{x}^{T}}\right]\left({g_\mu(\bm{x}) \cdot g_\nu(\bm{x})}\right),
    \qquad \forall T\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:log-concave}
A nonzero polynomial $g$ with nonnegative coefficients is
\emph{log-concave} on $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$ if
\begin{align*}
    \nabla^2\log g(\bm{x}) \preceq 0, \qquad\forall \bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:log-concave-convolution}
Let $\mu,\nu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ be two nonnegative weight functions given by evaluation oracles,\footnote{This means that there is a black-box that returns the weight $\mu(S)$ (resp. $\nu(S)$) on input $S \subseteq {\mathcal{U}}$. The number of calls to this black-box is counted in the overall running time of our algorithms.} and suppose $g_\mu,g_\nu$ are log-concave. Assume initial sets $S_{0},T_{0} \subseteq {\mathcal{U}}$ satisfying $\mu(S_{0})>0,\nu(T_{0})>0$, upper bounds on ${\mathcal{R}}_\mu,{\mathcal{R}}_\nu$, and an error parameter $0 < \varepsilon \leq 1$ are given. Then there is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for any specified coefficient
\begin{align*}
 Z_{\bm{\alpha}} \coloneqq \left[{\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}}\right]\left({g_\mu(\bm{x}) \cdot g_\nu(\bm{x})}\right),
 \qquad \bm{\alpha}\in\{0,1,2\}^{{\mathcal{U}}}
\end{align*}
that uses at most
\begin{align*}
    \widetilde{O}\left({\frac{n^{11} \cdot \left({n + \log({\mathcal{R}}_{\mu} \cdot {\mathcal{R}}_{\nu})}\right)^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}}\right)
\end{align*}
arithmetic operations and evaluation oracle calls.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
This is an immediate corollary of \cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} in the case $\bm{\alpha} = \mathbf{1}$ by setting $\mu(S) = \mathbf{1}[S \in {\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{M}})]$ and $\nu(T) = \mathbf{1}[{\mathcal{U}} \setminus T \in {\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{N}})]$, both of which can be evaluated given independence oracles for ${\mathcal{M}},{\mathcal{N}}$. Log-concavity of $g_{\mu},g_{\nu}$ was established in \cite{AnariOveisGharanVinzant2018,BrandenHuh2020}, and we can find initializing sets $S_{0},T_{0}$ by greedy algorithms.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:hadamard}
Let $\rho = \mu \odot \nu$ denote the probability measure supported on $\Omega$ defined by $(\mu \odot \nu)(S) \propto \mu(S) \cdot \nu(S)$ for all $S \subseteq {\mathcal{U}}$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
${\mathscr{L}}_{u}$ is reversible with respect to $\rho$ for all $u \in {\mathcal{U}}$, i.e. $\langle f, {\mathscr{L}}_{u}g \rangle_{\rho} = \langle {\mathscr{L}}_{u}f, g \rangle_{\rho}$ for all functions $f,g : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$. Moreover, ${\mathscr{L}}_{u}$ is positive semidefinite, i.e. $\langle f, {\mathscr{L}}_{u} f \rangle_{\rho} \geq 0$ for all $f : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$.
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:discrete-chain}
The continuous-time chain with generator $-{\mathscr{L}}$ can be simulated by a
simple discrete-time chain. Let $B\ge\max_{S\in\Omega,\,u\in{\mathcal{U}}}|r_u(S)|$
be any known bound on the rates. From the current state $S\in\Omega$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),nosep,leftmargin=2em]
 \item With probability $1/2$, stay at $S$.
 \item Otherwise, choose $u\in{\mathcal{U}}$ uniformly at random, and
 \begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item if $u\notin S$ and $S+u\in\Omega$, move to $S+u$ with probability
  $\mu(S+u)/(B\mu(S))$;
  \item if $u\in S$ {and $S-u\in\Omega$}, move to $S-u$ with probability $\nu(S-u)/(B\nu(S))$;
  \item otherwise, stay at $S$.
 \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
Each probability in (2) is at most $1$ by the choice of $B$. The
resulting transition matrix is $P=I-{\mathscr{L}}/(2nB)$, which is lazy and
reversible with respect to $\rho$, and its spectral gap is that of ${\mathscr{L}}$
divided by $2nB$. The Poincar\'e inequality below therefore gives the
mixing bound \cref{eq:poincare-mixing} with $R=nB$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:spectral-curvature}
Fix a parameter $\kappa \in {\mathbb{R}}$. For a nonnegative weight function $\mu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ that is not identically zero, and each $S \in \operatorname{supp}(\mu)$, define the ${\mathcal{U}} \times {\mathcal{U}}$ \emph{(upward) $\kappa$-curvature matrix}\footnote{Note that the only nonzero entries $A_{S}^{\mu}$ come from elements in ${\mathcal{U}} \setminus S$.}
\begin{align*}
    A_{S}^{\mu,\kappa}(u,v) \coloneqq \begin{cases}
        \frac{\mu(S + v)^{2}}{\mu(S)^{2}} - \kappa \cdot \frac{\mu(S + v)}{\mu(S)}, &\quad\text{if } u,v \notin S, u = v \\
        \frac{\mu(S + u)}{\mu(S)} \cdot \frac{\mu(S + v)}{\mu(S)} - \frac{\mu(S + u + v)}{\mu(S)}, &\quad\text{if } u,v \notin S, u \neq v \\
        0, &\quad\text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
\end{align*}
We say $\mu$ has \emph{(upward) $\kappa$-spectral curvature} if $A_{S}^{\mu,\kappa} \succeq 0$ for every $S \in \operatorname{supp}(\mu)$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
In this paper, we are primarily interested in the $\kappa \geq 0$ regime. However, we note that $\kappa$ can be any real number; see \cref{app:curvature-examples} for examples.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Unlike the influence/correlation/covariance matrices appearing in the theory of spectral independence \cite{ALO2020} and localization schemes \cite{ChenEldan2022}, whose entries are $\#\mathsf{P}$-hard to compute exactly, the entries of $A_{S}^{\mu,\kappa}$ are straightforward to compute for any $S \in \operatorname{supp}(\mu)$. Hence, for many applications, verifying spectral curvature can be done easily by hand.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:dual-measure}
Let $\mu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ be nonzero. We define its \emph{dual} $\mu^{*} : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ by $\mu^{*}(S) \coloneqq \mu({\mathcal{U}} \setminus S)$ for all $S \subseteq {\mathcal{U}}$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:poincare}
Let $\mu,\nu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ have {a common nonempty support $\Omega$, connected under single-element additions and deletions}, and let $\rho = \mu \odot \nu$ be their Hadamard product, which is supported on $\Omega$. If $\mu$ has $\eta$-spectral curvature and $\nu^{*}$ has $\kappa$-spectral curvature, where $\eta,\kappa \in {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfy $\eta + \kappa > 0$, then $\rho$ obeys the Poincar\'{e} Inequality
\begin{align*}
    (\eta + \kappa) \cdot  \ifthenelse{\isempty{\rho}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\rho}\left[f\right]}  \leq \langle f, {\mathscr{L}} f \rangle_{\rho}, \qquad \forall f : \Omega \to {\mathbb{R}}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:positive-curvature-support}, a positive spectral-gap bound from \cref{thm:poincare} forces $\Omega$ to be upward or downward closed after removing coordinates that are constant on $\Omega$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:curvature-convolution}
Suppose $\mu,\nu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ have downward closed supports and upward spectral curvatures $\eta,\kappa$, with $\eta+\kappa\ge0$.
Put $\gamma\coloneqq \max\{\eta,\kappa\}$; if $\gamma>0$,
let $\chi\ge1$ be a supplied bound, polynomial in $n$, such that, for each
$\omega\in\{\mu,\nu\}$,
\begin{align*}
 \omega(S+u)&\le\chi \cdot \gamma \cdot \omega(S),
 \qquad \forall S\in\operatorname{supp}\omega, \, \forall u\notin S.
\end{align*}
In all other cases, take $\chi=1$ without imposing this bound.
Given value oracles for $\mu,\nu$, upper bounds on ${\mathcal{R}}_\mu,{\mathcal{R}}_\nu$, and an error parameter $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, there is an
$\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for any specified coefficient
\begin{align*}
 Z_{\bm{\alpha}}&\coloneqq [\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}]\bigl(g_\mu(\bm{x}) \cdot g_\nu(\bm{x})\bigr),
 \qquad \bm{\alpha}\in\{0,1,2\}^{{\mathcal{U}}}
\end{align*}
that uses at most
\begin{align*}
 \widetilde{O}\left({\frac{n^{11}(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))^2}{\varepsilon^2}
       +\frac{n^5\chi(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))}{\varepsilon^3}}\right)
\end{align*}
arithmetic operations and evaluation oracle calls.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rmk:curvature-LC-generalization}
                                                                            
\Cref{thm:curvature-convolution} can be viewed as a generalization of
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}. For log-concave measures, translating
$g_\mu(\bm{x}),g_\nu(\bm{x})$ to
$g_\mu(\mathbf1+\bm{x}),g_\nu(\mathbf1+\bm{x})$ gives downward-closed measures
with zero curvature by \cref{prop:flc-curvature}.
After reducing to homogeneous polynomials whose degrees sum to $n$
(see \cref{app:convolution-proofs}), these translations preserve the
coefficient of $\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$. The translated weights, i.e. the coefficients of $g_{\mu}(\mathbf{1} + \bm{x}), g_{\nu}(\mathbf{1} + \bm{x})$, are respectively
\[
 \widehat\mu(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\mu(T),
 \qquad \widehat\nu(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}\nu(T).
\]
These sums each admit an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ since $\mu,\nu$ are log-concave~\cite{AnariEtAl2019}.
Using sufficiently accurate estimates of the queried weights and
controlling the accumulated sampling error gives the reduction,
with additional polynomial overhead. We state
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} separately to give a direct
algorithm using the original evaluation oracles and a sharper
running-time bound.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rmk:curvature-threshold}
The condition $\eta+\kappa\ge0$ in \cref{thm:curvature-convolution}
is optimal among constant lower bounds on the curvature sum.
For every fixed $\delta>0$, there is no $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ under the
weaker condition $\eta+\kappa>-\delta$, unless
$\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$. This holds even when $\mu=\nu$ have
downward-closed support, polynomial-time value oracles, and
$\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)=O(n\log n)$.
The proof is deferred to \cref{app:curvature-threshold}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:pairwise-dependency}
Let $S\in\operatorname{supp}(\mu)$. The \emph{pairwise dependency matrix} of $\mu$
at $S$ is the symmetric matrix $M_S$ with entries
\begin{align*}
 M_S(u,v)&\coloneqq
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{\mu(S+u+v) \cdot \mu(S)}{\mu(S+u) \cdot \mu(S+v)}-1,&u\ne v,\\
 0,&u=v.
 \end{cases}
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
For $\delta>0$, the $\delta$-ultra-log-concavity of
\cite[Definition~3.5]{ChenWang2026} extends this criterion to measures
on $\mathbb N^{{\mathcal{U}}}$ with downward-closed support.
On the Boolean cube, it is exactly upward $(\delta-1)$-spectral
curvature; the case $\delta=1$ corresponds to zero upward curvature.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:fractional-log-concavity}
Let $0<\alpha\le1$, and let $p\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
be a nonzero polynomial with nonnegative coefficients.
We say that $p$ is \emph{$\alpha$-fractionally log-concave} if
$\bm{x}\mapsto\log p(x_1^\alpha,\ldots,x_n^\alpha)$ is concave on
$\mathbb R_{>0}^n$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:flc-curvature}
Let $p$ be nonzero, multiaffine, and $\alpha$-fractionally log-concave,
with nonnegative coefficients and $0<\alpha\le1$. The coefficient
measure $\widehat\mu$ defined by
$g_{\widehat\mu}(\bm{x})\coloneqq p(\mathbf1+\bm{x})$ has downward-closed support and
upward $(1-\alpha^{-1})$-spectral curvature.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
Lorentzian polynomials extend the theory of multi-affine homogeneous log-concave polynomials to polynomials with $\mathrm M$-convex supports
\cite[Theorems~2.30 and~3.10]{BrandenHuh2020}.
For a nonzero multiaffine Lorentzian polynomial $p$,
\cref{prop:flc-curvature} with $\alpha=1$ gives zero upward spectral
curvature for the coefficient measure of $p(\mathbf1+\bm{x})$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:zero-curvature-log-concavity}
Let $\mu : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}_{\geq0}$ have downward closed support. If $\mu$ has (upward) $0$-spectral curvature, then $g_\mu$ is log-concave.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:bochner-criterion}
Let ${\mathcal{L}}$ be the Laplacian of an irreducible reversible Markov chain on
a finite state space $\Omega$, with stationary distribution $\pi$. Then
its spectral gap satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \gamma\coloneqq \inf_{f\text{ nonconstant}}
   \frac{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}{ \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right]} }
 &=\inf_{f\text{ nonconstant}}
   \frac{\langle{\mathcal{L}} f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:homogeneous-convolution-informal}
Let $\mu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ and
$\nu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, extended by zero to $2^{{\mathcal{U}}}$,
where $a,b\ge0$ are integers with $a+b=n\coloneqq |{\mathcal{U}}|\ge1$.
Suppose $g_\mu,g_\nu$ are log-concave. Given value oracles for $\mu,\nu$,
the coefficient ranges ${\mathcal{R}}_\mu,{\mathcal{R}}_\nu$, and one set in the support of
each measure, there is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for the subset-convolution value
\begin{align*}
 Z_\cap&\coloneqq (\mu\ast\nu)({\mathcal{U}})=[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_\mu(\bm{x}) \cdot g_\nu(\bm{x})\bigr)
       =\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\cdot\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S).
\end{align*}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rmk:penalty-alone}
An inverse-polynomial $t$ need not give complementary pairs
inverse-polynomial probability when $\bm{z}=\mathbf1$. Consider the
following ladder of Jerrum, Sinclair, and
Vigoda~\cite[Figure~2]{JerrumSinclairVigoda2004}.
                     
                                                         
Blue $S$ and orange $B={\mathcal{U}}\setminus T$ are bases of the partition matroids
on filled and hollow vertices, respectively; shared edges are drawn twice
above and once below.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c@{}}

   \foreach \i in {0,...,4} {\draw[edge] (\i,0)--(\i,1);}
                                                                      
   \ifnum\panel=0
    \foreach \xa/\ya/\xb/\yb in {
      -.7/1/0/1,4/0/4.7/0,0/0/1/0,2/0/3/0,1/1/2/1,3/1/4/1} {
     \draw[leftbasis] (\xa,\ya) to[bend left=13] (\xb,\yb);
     \draw[rightbasis] (\xa,\ya) to[bend right=13] (\xb,\yb);
    }
   \else
    \foreach \xa/\ya/\xb/\yb in {
      0/0/0/1,1/0/1/1,2/0/3/0,2/1/3/1,4/0/4/1} {

 }

 every node/.style={font=\footnotesize}]
 \foreach \panel in {0,1} {
  \begin{scope}[xshift=\panel*6.4cm]
   \ifnum\panel=1
    \fill[black!6] (-.18,-.18) rectangle (1.18,1.18);
    \fill[black!6] (1.82,-.18) rectangle (3.18,1.18);
   \fi
   \draw[edge] (-.7,1)--(0,1)--(4,1) (0,0)--(4,0)--(4.7,0);
   \foreach \i in {0,...,4} {\draw[edge] (\i,0)--(\i,1);}
   \ifnum\panel=0
    \draw[matched] (-.7,1)--(0,1) (4,0)--(4.7,0)
      (0,0)--(1,0) (2,0)--(3,0) (1,1)--(2,1) (3,1)--(4,1);
   \else
    \draw[matched] (0,0)--(0,1) (1,0)--(1,1)
      (2,0)--(3,0) (2,1)--(3,1) (4,0)--(4,1);
   \fi
   \foreach \i in {0,...,4} {
    \node[vertex] at (\i,0) {}; \node[vertex] at (\i,1) {};
   }
   \ifnum\panel=0
    \node[vertex] at (-.7,1) {}; \node[vertex] at (4.7,0) {};
    \node[align=center] at (2,-.65) {Unique perfect matching};
   \else
    \node[freevertex] at (-.7,1) {}; \node[freevertex] at (4.7,0) {};
    \node[align=center] at (2,-.65) {Leaves unmatched: two choices per shaded block};
   \fi
  \end{scope}
 }
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The pendant edges force a unique perfect matching $M$. Leaving both
leaves unmatched gives exponentially many near-perfect matchings $C$,
with two choices per shaded block. Completing $C$ as shown gives a
distinct soft configuration with $|S\cap T|=|S\setminus B|=1$,
hence only one factor of $t$. Their total weight makes the perfect matching exponentially unlikely.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:Phi-program}
Fix $t\in(0,1]$. Write the external field as $\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}$,
where $\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$ gives its logarithmic coordinates, and define
\begin{align}\label{eq:field-gradient}
 \Phi(\bm{y})&\coloneqq \log Z_{t,\bm{z}}-\sum_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}y_u,&
 \partial_u\Phi(\bm{y})&=\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(u\in S)-\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(u\notin T).
\end{align}
We consider the following convex program:
\begin{align} \label{eq:Phi-program}
    \inf_{\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\Phi(\bm{y}).
\end{align}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:field-concavity}
Let $\gamma>0$. Suppose that for every $\bm{t}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}}$ and
$\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, there is an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain
reversible with respect to $\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$, with spectral gap at least $\gamma$.
Each move updates only one of the two sets $S,T$.
Whenever $u\in S\oplus T$, the total rate of moves removing
its unique copy is at most $1$. Then for every scalar $t\in(0,1]$ and every
$\bm{z}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, with $\bm{y}=\log\bm{z}$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:field-certificate}
 \pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T\ne{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)
 &\le n\left(\|\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})\|_\infty+\frac{4\sqrt t}{\gamma}\right).
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rmk:partition-penalty}
The penalty $\psi_{\bm{t}}$ can be understood as an analogue of the
random-cluster model, where there is a soft penalty for non-independent
sets. Let $\mathcal P$ be the partition
matroid on ${\mathcal{U}}\times\{1,2\}$ allowing at most one copy of each $u$,
and set $X\coloneqq(S\times\{1\})\cup(T\times\{2\})$.
For uniform penalties $t_u=t\in(0,1]$,
\[
 \psi_{t\mathbf{1}}(S,T)=t^{|S\cap T|}
 =t^{|X|-{\mathsf{rk}_{\mathcal P}}(X)}.
\]
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rmk:gurvits-capacity}
For a nonzero finitely supported measure $w$ on $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n$,
write $g_w(\bm x)=\sum_{\bm k}w(\bm k)\bm x^{\bm k}$.
Its \emph{Gurvits capacity} at $\bm\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}^n$ is
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_{\bm\alpha}(g_w)\coloneqq
 \inf_{\bm x\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^n}\frac{g_w(\bm x)}{\bm x^{\bm\alpha}}.
\]
The Gurvits capacity at $\bm \alpha \in \operatorname{supp} w$ is always an upper bound on $w(\bm \alpha)$.
To see this, define the distribution
$p_{\bm z}(\bm k)=w(\bm k)\bm z^{\bm k}/g_w(\bm z)$.
If $\bm\alpha\in\operatorname{supp} w$, then
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_{\bm\alpha}(g_w)
 =\frac{w(\bm\alpha)}{\sup_{\bm z>0}p_{\bm z}(\bm\alpha)} \geq w(\bm \alpha).
\]
                                                                        
                                                                     
                 
Intuitively, it gives the best possible approximation of $w(\bm \alpha)$ that we can get by only tuning external fields applied to the base measure.

After taking logarithms, the optimization over external fields above has
a dual formulation as a minimum $\operatorname{KL}$-divergence convex program with prescribed mean,
or equivalently, a weighted maximum-entropy convex program~\cite{SinghVishnoi2014Entropy}.
For $\bm\alpha\in\operatorname{supp} w$, let
\[
 q^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q:\,\mathbb E_q[\bm X]=\bm\alpha}
 D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(q\,\middle\|\,p_{\mathbf{1}}\right),
\]
where $q$ ranges over probability distributions on $\operatorname{supp} w$,
$p_{\mathbf{1}}=w/g_w(\mathbf1)$ is the normalized measure, and
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ denotes Kullback--Leibler divergence.
Entropy duality and the KL Pythagorean identity~\cite[Theorem~3.2]{CsiszarShields2004}
give
\[
 \log\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\bm\alpha}(g_w)}{w(\bm\alpha)}
 =D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\delta_{\bm\alpha}\,\middle\|\,q^*\right)
 =-\log q^*(\bm\alpha),
\]
where $\delta_{\bm\alpha}$ is the point mass at $\bm\alpha$.
In other words, we adjust the original distribution as little as possible
in KL divergence to obtain mean $\bm\alpha$. The approximation ratio is
the reciprocal of the probability that this distribution assigns to
$\bm\alpha$ itself.

For every homogeneous \emph{real stable} polynomial $g$ of degree $n$ in $n$
variables with nonnegative coefficients,
\[
 \frac{n!}{n^n}\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(g)
 \le [x_1\cdots x_n]g
 \le \operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(g).
\]
The upper bound follows from the definition of capacity.
Gurvits~\cite{Gurvits2006} proves the lower bound, showing that capacity
overestimates the coefficient by at most a factor $n^n/n!$.
For the permanent of a nonnegative matrix $A$, he uses the polynomial
$g(\bm{x})=\prod_{i=1}^n(\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j)$;
for mixed discriminants, he uses
$g(\bm{x})=\det(\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i)$, where the $A_i$ are positive semidefinite.
This approach has since been extended to other settings; see
\cref{subsec:prior-work}.

In our setting, the target coefficient
$[\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]Z_{t,\bm{x}}=Z_\cap$ is independent of $t$.
For fixed $t$, the Gurvits capacity is
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})=
 \inf_{\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\frac{Z_{t,\bm{x}}}{\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}
 =\exp\left(\inf_{\bm{y}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}}\Phi(\bm{y})\right).
\]
When $Z_\cap>0$, the probability interpretation above gives the
approximation ratio
\[
 \frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(Z_{t,\bm x})}{Z_\cap}
 =\frac{1}{\sup_{\bm z>0}\pi_{t,\bm z}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)}.
\]
Under the hypotheses of \cref{lem:field-concavity}, this ratio satisfies
\[
 1\le\frac{\operatorname{Cap}_{\mathbf1}(Z_{t,\bm{x}})}{Z_\cap}
 \le\left(1-\frac{4n\sqrt t}{\gamma}\right)^{-1},
 \qquad 4n\sqrt t<\gamma.
\]
Indeed, $\Phi$ is bounded below and has a globally bounded Hessian,
so it admits points $\bm{y}$ with arbitrarily small gradient; applying
\cref{lem:field-concavity} to the corresponding fields $\bm{z}=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{y}}$
gives the upper bound on the ratio.
Thus decreasing $t$ makes the capacity bound nearly tight.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rmk:permanent-annealing}
\looseness=1
The permanent algorithm of Jerrum--Sinclair--Vigoda~\cite{JerrumSinclairVigoda2004}
learns correction weights along an annealing schedule to balance the total
weight of perfect matchings with that of each near-perfect class, indexed
by its pair of unmatched vertices.
Our framework chooses external fields directly by stochastic gradient
descent. It can serve as a black box for a broad class of counting
problems admitting the above formulation, once the sampling and uniform
Poincar\'e hypotheses are verified.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since the chain is reversible, ${\mathcal{L}}$ is self-adjoint and positive
semidefinite with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\pi$; since it
is irreducible, its kernel consists of the constant functions. Hence
${\mathcal{L}}$ is positive definite on $\mathbf1^\perp$
{(the functions with mean zero under $\pi$)}, and ${\mathcal{L}}^{1/2}$ is a
bijection of $\mathbf1^\perp$. Both ratios are unchanged when a constant
is added to $f$, so we may take $f\in\mathbf1^\perp\setminus\{0\}$, for
which $ \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[f\right]} =\langle f,f\rangle_\pi$. Substituting
$g\coloneqq{\mathcal{L}}^{1/2}f$ gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\langle{\mathcal{L}} f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}{\langle f,{\mathcal{L}} f\rangle_\pi}
 &=\frac{\langle g,{\mathcal{L}} g\rangle_\pi}{\langle g,g\rangle_\pi},
\end{align*}
and $g$ ranges over $\mathbf1^\perp\setminus\{0\}$ as $f$ does. Hence
the two infima coincide.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:sampling-to-counting}
Let $m\ge1$, let $w:\{0,1\}^m\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$ be nonzero, and write
$Z\coloneqq\sum_{\sigma}w(\sigma)$ and $\pi(\sigma)\coloneqq w(\sigma)/Z$.
For every nonempty conditional law obtained by fixing coordinates,
suppose a sampler, given any starting state in its support and an
accuracy $0<\tau<1$, returns
a sample in that support whose distribution is within total variation distance $\tau$ of
the conditional law, using fresh independent randomness.
Given an evaluation oracle for $w$, a state $\sigma_0\in\operatorname{supp} w$, and
$0<\varepsilon,\delta<1$, one can compute $\widehat Z$ satisfying
\[
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbf{Pr}\left[(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z\right]}
  {\mathbf{Pr}_{}\left[(1-\varepsilon)Z\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z\right]} \ge1-\delta.
\]
On every execution, the algorithm uses
$Q=O(m^3\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2m/\delta))$ sampler calls, each with total variation distance at most
$\tau=\varepsilon/(16m)$, one evaluation of $w$, and $O(Q)$ additional
arithmetic operations. It supplies a starting state for every call.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:stochastic-coordinate-descent}
Fix $d\ge1$, $\bm{x}_0\in\mathbb R^d$, $L,\sigma>0$, and $H_0\ge0$.
Assume the following.
\begingroup
\setlist[enumerate,1]{label=(\roman*),wide=0pt}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Function.} The function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$
is convex and differentiable, and for all $\bm{x}\in\mathbb R^d$,
$u\in\mathbb R$, and $1\le i\le d$,
\begin{align}
 f(\bm{x}+u\bm{e}_i)&\le f(\bm{x})+u\partial_i f(\bm{x})+Lu^2/2,\label{eq:coordinate-smoothness}\\
 f(\bm{x})&\ge f(\bm{x}_0)-H_0.\label{eq:coordinate-lower-bound}
\end{align}
Here $(\bm{e}_i)_j\coloneqq \mathbf{1}_{\{i=j\}}$.
\item \textbf{Gradient oracle.} Each query at $\bm{x}$ uses fresh independent
randomness and costs at most $T\ge d$. Its output $\bm{G}(\bm{x})$ is unbiased
with coordinatewise $\sigma$-sub-Gaussian noise: for all $\bm{x},u,i$ as above,
\begin{align*}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[\bm{G}(\bm{x})\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[\bm{G}(\bm{x})\right]} &=\nabla f(\bm{x}),\\
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\bigl(u(G_i(\bm{x})-\partial_i f(\bm{x}))\bigr)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[\exp\bigl(u(G_i(\bm{x})-\partial_i f(\bm{x}))\bigr)\right]} 
 &\le\exp(\sigma^2u^2/2).
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}
For any $0<\eta\le1$ and $0<\delta<1$, a stochastic coordinate-descent
algorithm has the following guarantees.
\setlist[enumerate,1]{label=(\alph*),wide=0pt}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Output and queries.} With probability at least $1-\delta$,
it returns $\bm{x}$ with $\|\nabla f(\bm{x})\|_\infty\le\eta$.
On every execution, every queried or returned point $\bm{y}$ satisfies
\begin{align}
 \|\bm{y}-\bm{x}_0\|_1&=O\left(\frac{H_0}{\eta}+\frac{\eta}{L}\right).\label{eq:scd-iterates}
\end{align}
\item \textbf{Cost.} On every execution, it uses $O(Q)$ oracle calls
and total time $O(TQ)$, where
\begin{align}
 Q&\coloneqq \left(1+\frac{\sigma^2}{\eta^2}\right)
       \left(1+\frac{LH_0}{\eta^2}\right)
       \log\left[\frac{2d}{\delta}
                   \left(1+\frac{LH_0}{\eta^2}\right)\right].\label{eq:scd-budget}
\end{align}
\end{enumerate}
\endgroup
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:approximate-sampling}
If the $j$th oracle output, conditional on the history, is within total
variation distance $\xi_j$ of its prescribed law, then the conclusion of
\cref{thm:stochastic-coordinate-descent}(a) holds with probability at
least $1-\delta-\sum_j\xi_j$, and the remaining guarantees hold on every
execution. Indeed, coupling each output with an exact one, the two runs
agree except with probability at most $\sum_j\xi_j$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:discrete-gradient}
For each $u \in {\mathcal{U}}$ and $f : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$, let
\begin{align*}
    (\nabla_{u}f)(S) \coloneqq f(S + u) - f(S - u).
\end{align*}
Further define the upper and lower discrete derivatives via
\begin{align*}
    (\nabla_{u}^{+}f)(S) \coloneqq (\nabla_{u}f)(S) \cdot \mathbf{1}[u \notin S] \qquad\text{and}\qquad (\nabla_{u}^{-}f)(S) \coloneqq (\nabla_{u}f)(S) \cdot \mathbf{1}[u \in S].
\end{align*}
Note that $(\nabla f)(S), (\nabla^{+}f)(S), (\nabla^{-}f)(S)$ are vectors in ${\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:bochner-identity}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{thm:poincare}, for every function $f : 2^{{\mathcal{U}}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$, we have the identity,
\begin{align*}
    \left\langle{f, \left({\mathscr{L}^{2} - (\eta + \kappa) \cdot \mathscr{L}}\right) f}\right\rangle_{\rho} &= \sum_{S\in\Omega} \rho(S) \cdot (\nabla^{+}f)(S)^{\top} \cdot A_{S}^{\mu,\eta} \cdot (\nabla^{+}f)(S) \\
    &+ \sum_{S\in\Omega} \rho(S) \cdot (\nabla^{-}f)(S)^{\top} \cdot D_{S}^{\nu,\kappa} \cdot (\nabla^{-}f)(S) \\
    &+ \frac{1}{Z} \sum_{S\in\Omega} \sum_{\substack{u,v\notin S : u\neq v\\S+u+v\in\Omega}} \mu(S + u + v) \cdot \nu(S) \cdot (\Delta_{uv}f)(S)^{2},
\end{align*}
where
\begin{align*}
    (\Delta_{uv}f)(S) \coloneqq (\nabla_{u}\nabla_{v}f)(S) = f(S + u + v) - f(S + u - v) - f(S - u + v) + f(S - u - v),
\end{align*}
and $Z = \sum_{S \subseteq {\mathcal{U}}} \mu(S) \cdot \nu(S)$ is the normalizing constant for $\rho$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
In \Cref{prop:bochner-identity}, the term $(\Delta_{uv}f)(S)^2$ is non-negative automatically; and, by the spectral-curvature conditions, the first two terms are also non-negative.
Hence $\langle{\mathscr{L}} f,{\mathscr{L}} f\rangle_\rho\ge(\eta+\kappa) \cdot \langle f,{\mathscr{L}} f\rangle_\rho$
for all $f$. The chain generated by $-{\mathscr{L}}$ is reversible with respect
to $\rho$ and irreducible on $\Omega$, since $\Omega$ is
connected under single-element additions and deletions and every feasible
transition has positive rate. Thus \cref{prop:bochner-criterion} gives
spectral gap $\gamma\ge\eta+\kappa$, which is the desired Poincar\'e
inequality.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We show that subtracting the two curvature terms leaves a weighted
sum of squares of the mixed second differences $\Delta_{uv}f$,
the off-diagonal entries of the discrete Hessian of $f$.
Let $S\sim\rho$ and write
$\bm{r}(S)\coloneqq (r_u(S))_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}$,
where $r_u(S)$ is defined just before \cref{eq:full-laplacian}.
Since $r_u(S)$ is signed, the vector
of nonnegative transition rates is $|\bm{r}(S)|\coloneqq (|r_u(S)|)_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}$.
Self-adjointness and \cref{eq:dirichlet-form} give
\begin{align*}
 \left\langle f, {\mathscr{L}}^2f\right\rangle_\rho
 &=\left\langle {\mathscr{L}} f, {\mathscr{L}} f\right\rangle_\rho
 = \ifthenelse{\isempty{S \sim \rho}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top \bm{r}(S)\bm{r}(S)^\top(\nabla f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{S \sim \rho}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top \bm{r}(S)\bm{r}(S)^\top(\nabla f)(S)\right]} ,\\
 \left\langle f, {\mathscr{L}} f\right\rangle_\rho
 &=\frac12 \cdot  \ifthenelse{\isempty{S \sim \rho}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top\operatorname{diag}(|\bm{r}(S)|)(\nabla f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{S \sim \rho}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top\operatorname{diag}(|\bm{r}(S)|)(\nabla f)(S)\right]} .
\end{align*}
Detailed balance pairs each addition with its reverse deletion, so
\begin{align*}
 \left\langle f, {\mathscr{L}} f\right\rangle_\rho
 &= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla^+f)(S)^\top\operatorname{diag}(|\bm{r}(S)|)(\nabla^+f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla^+f)(S)^\top\operatorname{diag}(|\bm{r}(S)|)(\nabla^+f)(S)\right]} \\
 &= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla^-f)(S)^\top\operatorname{diag}(|\bm{r}(S)|)(\nabla^-f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla^-f)(S)^\top\operatorname{diag}(|\bm{r}(S)|)(\nabla^-f)(S)\right]} .
\end{align*}
Define the matrix
\begin{align*}
 B_S&\coloneqq \operatorname{offdiag}\bigl(\bm{r}(S)\bm{r}(S)^\top-A_S^{\mu,\eta}-D_S^{\nu,\kappa}\bigr),
\end{align*}
where $\operatorname{offdiag}(M)$ sets the diagonal entries of $M$ to zero.
Subtracting the two curvature terms from the left-hand side gives
\begin{align*}
 \left\langle f, ({\mathscr{L}}^2-(\eta+\kappa){\mathscr{L}})f\right\rangle_\rho
 &- \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla^+f)(S)^\top A_S^{\mu,\eta}(\nabla^+f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla^+f)(S)^\top A_S^{\mu,\eta}(\nabla^+f)(S)\right]} 
 - \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla^-f)(S)^\top D_S^{\nu,\kappa}(\nabla^-f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla^-f)(S)^\top D_S^{\nu,\kappa}(\nabla^-f)(S)\right]} \\
 &= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top B_S(\nabla f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top B_S(\nabla f)(S)\right]} .
\end{align*}
The diagonal terms cancel using the
preceding Dirichlet-form identities and the definitions of
$A_S^{\mu,\eta}$ and $D_S^{\nu,\kappa}$.
 
Expanding the expectation gives
\begin{align*}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top B_S(\nabla f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top B_S(\nabla f)(S)\right]} 
 &=\sum_{X\in\Omega}\sum_{\substack{u,v\in{\mathcal{U}}:\,u\ne v}}
   \rho(X)B_X(u,v)(\nabla_u f)(X)(\nabla_v f)(X).
\end{align*}

{
Whenever $S,T=S+u+v\in\Omega$ for distinct $u,v\notin S$, both
$S+u$ and $S+v$ also belong to $\Omega$.
Indeed, if $\mu(S+u)=0$, then $A_S^{\mu,\eta}(u,u)=0$ but
$A_S^{\mu,\eta}(u,v)=-\mu(T)/\mu(S)\ne0$, contradicting positive
semidefiniteness. The other intermediate set is handled symmetrically.}

\begin{observation}\label{obs:bochner-coefficients}
For $S\in\Omega$ and distinct $u,v\notin S$ with $T\coloneqq S+u+v\in\Omega$,
set $w\coloneqq \mu(T)\nu(S)/Z$. Then
\begin{align*}
 \rho(S)B_S(u,v)&=\rho(T)B_T(u,v)
 =-\rho(S+u)B_{S+u}(u,v)=-\rho(S+v)B_{S+v}(u,v)=w.
\end{align*}
\end{observation}

We regroup by $S=X-u-v$, writing $T=S+u+v$.
{For each $X\in\{S,S+u,S+v,T\}\cap\Omega$, direct substitution gives
$\rho(X)B_X(u,v)=\pm\mu(T)\nu(S)/Z$.
This vanishes unless both $S,T\in\Omega$, since the two measures have
common support. In that case, both intermediate sets are supported
by the argument above.}
Thus
\begin{align*}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top B_S(\nabla f)(S)\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[(\nabla f)(S)^\top B_S(\nabla f)(S)\right]} 
 &=\sum_{S\in\Omega}
   \sum_{\substack{u,v\notin S:\,u\ne v\\T=S+u+v\in\Omega}}
   \sum_{X\in\{S,S+u,S+v,T\}}
   \rho(X)B_X(u,v)(\nabla_u f)(X)(\nabla_v f)(X).
\end{align*}
The gradient $\nabla_u f$ is unchanged when $u$ is added or removed,
and similarly for $\nabla_v f$. Thus \cref{obs:bochner-coefficients} gives, for each group,
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_{X\in\{S,S+u,S+v,T\}}
   \rho(X)B_X(u,v)(\nabla_u f)(X)(\nabla_v f)(X)\\
 &=w \cdot \bigl((\nabla_u f)(T)-(\nabla_u f)(S)\bigr)
      \bigl((\nabla_v f)(T)-(\nabla_v f)(S)\bigr)
 =w \cdot (\Delta_{uv}f)(S)^2.
\end{align*}
The last equality holds because each of the two differences equals
$(\nabla_u\nabla_v f)(S)=(\Delta_{uv}f)(S)$.
 
Substituting into the regrouped sum finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- observation-1: body_md -->
\label{obs:bochner-coefficients}
For $S\in\Omega$ and distinct $u,v\notin S$ with $T\coloneqq S+u+v\in\Omega$,
set $w\coloneqq \mu(T)\nu(S)/Z$. Then
\begin{align*}
 \rho(S)B_S(u,v)&=\rho(T)B_T(u,v)
 =-\rho(S+u)B_{S+u}(u,v)=-\rho(S+v)B_{S+v}(u,v)=w.
\end{align*}
<!-- end observation-1 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:homogeneous-convolution}
Let $\mu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ and
$\nu:\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, extended by zero to $2^{{\mathcal{U}}}$,
where $a,b\ge0$ are integers with $a+b=n\coloneqq |{\mathcal{U}}|\ge1$.
Suppose $g_\mu,g_\nu$ are log-concave. Given value oracles for $\mu,\nu$,
the coefficient ranges ${\mathcal{R}}_\mu,{\mathcal{R}}_\nu$ in
\cref{eq:coefficient-range}, and sets $S_0,T_0$ with
$\mu(S_0)>0$ and $\nu(T_0)>0$, there is an $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ for the
subset-convolution value $(\mu*\nu)({\mathcal{U}})$, namely
\begin{align}\label{def:Z-cap}
 Z_\cap&\coloneqq [\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_\mu(\bm{x})g_\nu(\bm{x})\bigr)
       =\sum_{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(S)\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S),
 \qquad \bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}\coloneqq \prod_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}x_u.
\end{align}
For every $0<\varepsilon\le1$, it uses at most
\begin{align}\label{eq:main-cost}
 O\left(n^{10}(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))^2\varepsilon^{-2}
       \log^2\frac{2(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))}{\varepsilon}\right)
\end{align}
arithmetic operations and value-oracle calls on every execution.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:independent-pair}
Let $\mu,\nu$ be as in \cref{thm:homogeneous-convolution},
$\bm{t}=(t_u)_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, and $\bm{z}\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$.
Write $\bm{z}\bm{x}\coloneqq (z_ux_u)_{u\in{\mathcal{U}}}$ and, for $R\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$,
$\bm{z}^R\coloneqq \prod_{u\in R}z_u$ and $\bm{t}^R\coloneqq \prod_{u\in R}t_u$.
{Define the weights $\widehat\mu_{\bm{z}},\widehat\nu_{\bm{z}}$ through
their generating polynomials by}
\begin{align*}
 g_{\widehat\mu_{\bm{z}}}(\bm{x})&\coloneqq g_\mu(\mathbf1+\bm{z}\bm{x}),&
 g_{\widehat\nu_{\bm{z}}}(\bm{x})&\coloneqq g_\nu(\mathbf1+\bm{z}\bm{x}).
\end{align*}
Write $(\widehat\mu_{\bm{z}}\otimes\widehat\nu_{\bm{z}})(S,T)
\coloneqq \widehat\mu_{\bm{z}}(S)\widehat\nu_{\bm{z}}(T)$ and $\psi_{\bm{t}}(S,T)\coloneqq \bm{t}^{S\cap T}$.
The \emph{independent-set pair law}
on $2^{{\mathcal{U}}}\times2^{{\mathcal{U}}}$ is the normalized Hadamard product
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}
 &\coloneqq (\widehat\mu_{\bm{z}}\otimes\widehat\nu_{\bm{z}})\odot\psi_{\bm{t}}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rmk:completion-weights}
Explicitly, for $S,T\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$,
\[
 \widehat\mu_{\bm{z}}(S)
 =\bm{z}^S\sum_{S\subseteq A\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\mu(A),
 \qquad
 \widehat\nu_{\bm{z}}(T)
 =\bm{z}^T\sum_{T\subseteq B\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\nu(B).
\]
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:pair-law}
With $\mu,\nu,\bm{t},\bm{z}$ as in \cref{def:independent-pair}, set
$\Omega\coloneqq \binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{a}\times\binom{{\mathcal{U}}}{b}$.
The \emph{bases pair law} is
$\widehat\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$ conditioned on $\Omega$.
Its partition function and probability mass function are
\begin{align*}
 Z_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}
 &\coloneqq \sum_{(S,T)\in\Omega}\mu(S)\nu(T)\bm{t}^{S\cap T}\bm{z}^S\bm{z}^T,\\
 \pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}(S,T)
 &\coloneqq \frac{\mu(S)\nu(T)\bm{t}^{S\cap T}\bm{z}^S\bm{z}^T}{Z_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:bases-pair-poincare}
Let $\bm{t}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, $\bm{z}\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, and let $\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$ be the
bases pair law of \cref{def:pair-law}. On $\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$, consider
the exchange chain with rates
\begin{align}\label{eq:pair-exchange-rates}
 q\bigl((S,T),(S-u+v,T)\bigr)
 &\coloneqq t_u^{-\mathbf{1}[u\in T]}
       \frac{z_v\mu(S-u+v)}
       {\sum_{w\in{\mathcal{U}}\setminus(S-u)}z_w\mu(S-u+w)},
\end{align}
where $u\in S$ and $v\notin S$.
The rates updating $T$ are obtained by interchanging $(S,\mu)$ and
$(T,\nu)$; all other off-diagonal rates are zero. This chain is
reversible with respect to $\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$ and satisfies
\begin{align}\label{eq:bases-pair-poincare}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}\left[f\right]} &\le{\mathcal{E}}_q(f,f), \quad \forall f:\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}\to\mathbb R.
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:bases-pair-sampling}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{lem:bases-pair-poincare} with a common
scalar penalty $t$, let $z_{\min}\coloneqq \min_u z_u$ and $z_{\max}\coloneqq \max_u z_u$.
Given a pair $(S_0,T_0)\in\operatorname{supp}\pi_{t,\bm{z}}$, the coefficient ranges
${\mathcal{R}}_\mu,{\mathcal{R}}_\nu$ in \cref{eq:coefficient-range}, and $0<\varepsilon<1$, one can sample
within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of $\pi_{t,\bm{z}}$ using
\begin{align*}
 O\left(\frac{n^2}{t}\left(
 n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)+n\log\frac{z_{\max}}{z_{\min}}
 +\min\{a,b\}\log\frac1t+\log\frac1\varepsilon\right)\right)
\end{align*}
arithmetic operations and calls to the value oracles for $\mu,\nu$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Apply \cref{eq:poincare-mixing} with $\gamma=1$ and $R=n/t$:
there are $a+b=n$ possible deletions, each with total rate at most $1/t$.
{Each step of the lazy discrete-time chain costs $O(n)$ operations and oracle calls:}
choose a present copy uniformly and, if it is $u\in S$, with probability
$t^{1-\mathbf{1}[u\in T]}/2$ resample it using the reinsertion weights in
\cref{eq:pair-exchange-rates}, allowing reinsertion of $u$; the update
of $T$ is symmetric. Since there are at most $4^n$ pairs, each of total
size $n$,
\begin{align*}
 \pi_{\min}
 &\ge\frac{t^{\min\{a,b\}}}{4^n{\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu}
       \left(\frac{z_{\min}}{z_{\max}}\right)^n.
\end{align*}
Substituting this bound and multiplying by the cost per step proves
the claim.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:independent-pair-poincare}
Let $\bm{t}\in(0,1]^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, $\bm{z}\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$, and $\lambda>0$.
Let ${\mathscr{L}}$ be the Laplacian in \cref{eq:full-laplacian} for the
factors $w_\lambda,\psi_{\bm{t}}$, and let $\widehat q_\lambda$ be its transition rates.
For every $F:\operatorname{supp}\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{t},\lambda \bm{z}}\to\mathbb R$, we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:independent-pair-poincare}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{\widehat\pi_{\bm{t},\lambda \bm{z}}}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[F\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\widehat\pi_{\bm{t},\lambda \bm{z}}}\left[F\right]} 
 &\le{\mathcal{E}}_{\widehat q_\lambda}(F,F)
 =\langle F,{\mathscr{L}} F\rangle_{\widehat\pi_{\bm{t},\lambda \bm{z}}}.
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- observation-2: body_md -->
\label{obs:w-0-curvature}
    $w_\lambda$ has $0$-spectral curvature.
<!-- end observation-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The generating polynomial of $w_\lambda$ is
    \begin{align*}
     g_{w_\lambda}(\bm{x},\bm{y})
     &=g_\mu(\mathbf1+\lambda \bm{z}\bm{x})\,
              g_\nu(\mathbf1+\lambda \bm{z}\bm{y}).
    \end{align*}
    Since $p(\bm{x},\bm{y})\coloneqq g_\mu(\bm{x})g_\nu(\bm{y})$ is log-concave,
    \cref{prop:flc-curvature} with $\alpha=1$ gives zero curvature for
    the coefficient measure of $p(\mathbf1+\bm{x},\mathbf1+\bm{y})$.
    {Positive rescaling of the variables preserves zero curvature:
    each curvature matrix $A$ becomes $DAD$, where $D$ is a diagonal matrix
    with positive entries, so positive semidefiniteness is preserved.}
    Applying the rescaling $(\bm{x},\bm{y})\mapsto(\lambda \bm{z}\bm{x},\lambda \bm{z}\bm{y})$
    therefore gives the assertion for
    $g_{w_\lambda}(\bm{x},\bm{y})=p(\mathbf1+\lambda \bm{z}\bm{x},\mathbf1+\lambda \bm{z}\bm{y})$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- observation-3: body_md -->
\label{obs:psi-star-1-curvature}
    $\psi_{\bm{t}}^*$ has $1$-spectral curvature.
<!-- end observation-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By definition, the dual measure $\psi_{\bm{t}}^*$ is
\begin{align*}
\psi_{\bm{t}}^*(S,T)
&\coloneqq \psi_{\bm{t}}({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S,{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T)
=\bm{t}^{{\mathcal{U}}\setminus(S\cup T)}
\mathbf{1}[({\mathcal{U}}\setminus S,{\mathcal{U}}\setminus T)\in\operatorname{supp}\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}].
\end{align*}
For $Y=(S,T)\in\operatorname{supp}\psi_{\bm{t}}^*$, downward closure of $\operatorname{supp}\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$
ensures that all additions to $Y$ remain supported.
Substitution into \cref{def:spectral-curvature} gives, for
$u,v\in{\mathcal{U}}$ and $i,j\in\{1,2\}$,
\begin{align*}
A_Y^{\psi_{\bm{t}}^*,1}\bigl((u,i),(v,j)\bigr)
&=\begin{cases}
(1-t_u)/t_u^2,& u=v,\ u\notin S\cup T,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
Here, we use $(u,1)$ and $(u,2)$ to denote that the element $u$ is added to $S$ and $T$, respectively.
Thus $A_Y^{\psi_{\bm{t}}^*,1}$ is a direct sum of zero blocks and blocks
$\frac{1-t_u}{t_u^2}\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$,
all positive semidefinite. Hence $\psi_{\bm{t}}^*$ has upward curvature one,
and \cref{thm:poincare} applies with $\eta=0$ and $\kappa=1$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Apply \cref{thm:poincare} to $w_\lambda\odot\psi_{\bm{t}}$ with
$(\eta,\kappa)=(0,1)$, using
\cref{obs:w-0-curvature,obs:psi-star-1-curvature}.
Normalizing the factors does not change their weight ratios.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:induced-chain}
Let $(X_s)_{s\ge0}$ be an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a
finite state space $\Omega$, with off-diagonal rates $r(x,y)$, and let
$\varnothing\ne B\subseteq\Omega$. Its \emph{induced chain on $B$} is the chain
obtained by deleting all time spent outside $B$. Writing
$\tau_B\coloneqq \inf\{s\ge0:X_s\in B\}$, its off-diagonal rates are
\begin{align*}
 r^B(x,y)&\coloneqq r(x,y)+\sum_{u\in\Omega\setminus B}
 r(x,u){ \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbf{Pr}\left[X_{\tau_B}=y\mid X_0=u\right]}
  {\mathbf{Pr}_{}\left[X_{\tau_B}=y\mid X_0=u\right]} }
 \qquad(x,y\in B,\ x\ne y).
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:induced-poincare}
In the setting of \cref{def:induced-chain}, suppose the chain is
reversible with stationary law $\pi$ and has spectral gap at least
$\gamma>0$. Then the induced chain is reversible with respect to
$\pi_B(x)\coloneqq \pi(x)/\pi(B)$ for $x\in B$, and for every $f:B\to\mathbb R$,
\begin{align*}
 \gamma \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi_B}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_B}\left[f\right]} &\le{\mathcal{E}}_{r^B}(f,f).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We pass to the induced chain on pairs of bases and show that its rates converge
to \cref{eq:pair-exchange-rates}. Singleton support is immediate.
Recall from \cref{eq:full-laplacian} that the chain with generator
$-{\mathscr{L}}$ has rates
\begin{align*}
 \widehat q_\lambda\bigl((S,T),(S+u,T)\bigr)
 &=\frac{w_\lambda(S+u,T)}{w_\lambda(S,T)}
 =\frac{\widehat\mu_{\lambda \bm{z}}(S+u)}{\widehat\mu_{\lambda \bm{z}}(S)}
 &&(u\notin S),\\
 \widehat q_\lambda\bigl((S,T),(S-u,T)\bigr)
 &=\frac{\psi_{\bm{t}}(S-u,T)}{\psi_{\bm{t}}(S,T)}
 =t_u^{-\mathbf{1}[u\in T]}
 &&(u\in S).
\end{align*}
The rates updating $T$ are symmetric; unsupported additions are
omitted and all other off-diagonal rates are zero.

Let $q_\lambda^{\mathrm{ind}}$ be the rates of the chain induced on
$\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$ from \cref{def:induced-chain}.
Conditioning $\widehat\pi_{\bm{t},\lambda \bm{z}}$ on pairs of bases cancels
the common factor $\lambda^n$, giving exactly $\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$.
By \cref{prop:induced-poincare,cor:independent-pair-poincare}, the induced chain
is therefore reversible with stationary law $\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$ and has
spectral gap at least one.

It remains to identify the limiting rates. After deleting $u\in S$
from a pair of bases $(S,T)$, put $S'\coloneqq S-u$. At $(S',T)$, additions
have positive total rate proportional to $\lambda$, whereas the
 total deletion rate is at most $n/\min_i t_i$. Thus the next jump is an
addition with probability $1-O(\lambda^{-1})$. Every such addition
returns to a pair of bases, and its conditional reinsertion law is
\begin{align*}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbf{Pr}\left[\text{reinsert }v\mid\text{next jump is an addition}\right]}
  {\mathbf{Pr}_{}\left[\text{reinsert }v\mid\text{next jump is an addition}\right]} 
 &=\frac{z_v\mu(S'+v)}{\sum_{w\notin S'}z_w\mu(S'+w)}
 \qquad(v\notin S').
\end{align*}
Multiplying by the initial deletion rate $t_u^{-\mathbf{1}[u\in T]}$
gives \cref{eq:pair-exchange-rates} in the limit. The same argument
applies to deletions from $T$; excursions with a further deletion
have probability $O(\lambda^{-1})$. Hence
$q_\lambda^{\mathrm{ind}}(X,Y)\to q(X,Y)$ for every distinct pair
$X,Y\in\operatorname{supp}\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}$.

Reversibility passes to the limit. Since the state space is finite,
passing to the limit in the induced chains' Poincar\'e inequalities
gives, for every $f$,
\begin{align*}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_{\bm{t},\bm{z}}}\left[f\right]} 
 &\le\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}{\mathcal{E}}_{q_\lambda^{\mathrm{ind}}}(f,f)
 ={\mathcal{E}}_q(f,f). \qedhere
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Fix $u$, and for $j \in \{0,1,2\}$, let $p_j$ be the probability under $\pi_{t,\bm{z}}$ that $u$ appears in exactly $j$ of the sets $S,T$. Since $p_2-p_0=\partial_u\Phi(\bm{y})$,
\begin{align*}
 p_0+p_2&\le|p_2-p_0|+2\sqrt{p_0p_2}
 =|\partial_u\Phi(\bm{y})|+2\sqrt{p_0p_2},
\end{align*}
so a union bound over $u$ reduces the lemma to
\begin{align*}
 p_0p_2&\le\frac{4t}{\gamma^2}\,p_1^2.
\end{align*}
Assume $p_0p_2>0$, and set $s\coloneqq \sqrt{tp_0/p_2}$. Remove the penalty at
$u$ and multiply $z_u$ by $s$: let $\bm{t}',\bm{z}'$ agree with $t\mathbf1,\bm{z}$
except at $u$, where $t'_u\coloneqq 1$ and $z'_u\coloneqq sz_u$. Then
\begin{align*}
 \pi_{\bm{t}',\bm{z}'}(S,T)&\propto\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(S,T)\cdot
 s^{\mathbf{1}[u\in S]+\mathbf{1}[u\in T]}\,t^{-\mathbf{1}[u\in S\cap T]},
\end{align*}
so the probabilities $q_0,q_1,q_2$ under $\pi_{\bm{t}',\bm{z}'}$ that $u$ lies in
exactly $0,1,2$ sets satisfy
\begin{align*}
 (q_0,q_1,q_2)&\propto(p_0,\,sp_1,\,s^2p_2/t)=(p_0,\,sp_1,\,p_0),
 \qquad\text{so }q_0=q_2\le\tfrac12.
\end{align*}
Let ${\mathcal{L}}'$ be the Laplacian supplied by the hypothesis for
$\pi_{\bm{t}',\bm{z}'}$. By assumption, the total rate of moves from one copy of
$u$ to none is at most $1$, and no move goes from two copies to none.
By reversibility, the Dirichlet form of
$g(S,T)\coloneqq \mathbf{1}[u\notin S\cup T]$ is therefore at most $q_1$.
The Poincar\'e inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 \gamma\,q_0(1-q_0)=\gamma \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi_{\bm{t}',\bm{z}'}}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[g\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_{\bm{t}',\bm{z}'}}\left[g\right]} 
 &\le\langle g,{\mathcal{L}}' g\rangle_{\pi_{\bm{t}',\bm{z}'}}\le q_1,
 &&\text{hence}&
 \frac\gamma2&\le\frac{q_1}{q_0}=\frac{\sqrt t\,p_1}{\sqrt{p_0p_2}}.
 \qedhere
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:balanced-fields}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{thm:homogeneous-convolution}, put
\begin{align*}
 t&\coloneqq \frac1{256n^2},&
 B&\coloneqq 2n+\lceil\log_2({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)\rceil.
\end{align*}
Given value oracles for $\mu,\nu$, the coefficient ranges ${\mathcal{R}}_\mu,{\mathcal{R}}_\nu$ in
\cref{eq:coefficient-range}, and a supported pair $(S_0,T_0)$,
there is a randomized algorithm that returns $\bm{z}\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{{\mathcal{U}}}$
or reports failure. If $Z_\cap>0$, with probability at least $31/32$
it returns a field satisfying
\begin{align*}
 \pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)&\ge\frac12.
\end{align*}
On every execution, it uses
$O(n^{10}B^2\log(2B))$ arithmetic operations and value-oracle calls,
and every queried or returned field satisfies
\begin{align}\label{eq:balancing-bounds}
 \|\log \bm{z}\|_1&=O(nB).
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:field-concavity}, it suffices to find $\bm{y}$ with
$\|\nabla\Phi(\bm{y})\|_\infty\le\eta\coloneqq 1/(4n)$ and return $\bm{z}\coloneqq \exp(\bm{y})$:
then $n(\eta+ 4\sqrt t)=1/2$. We apply
\cref{thm:stochastic-coordinate-descent} with
$d=n$, $L=\sigma=1$, $H_0=B$, and $\bm{x}_0=\bm{0}$.
For $(S,T)\sim\pi_{t,\exp(\bm{y})}$, the vector
$\bm{G}\coloneqq \mathbf1_S+\mathbf1_T-\mathbf1$ satisfies
\begin{align*}
 \nabla\Phi(\bm{y})&= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[\bm{G}\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[\bm{G}\right]} ,&
 \nabla^2\Phi(\bm{y})&=\operatorname{Cov}(\bm{G})\succeq0,\\
 \partial_u^2\Phi(\bm{y})&= \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[G_u\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{}\left[G_u\right]} \le1,&
 \bm{G}&\in[-1,1]^n.
\end{align*}
Thus $\Phi$ is convex and coordinatewise $1$-smooth, and Hoeffding's
lemma gives coordinatewise $1$-sub-Gaussian oracle noise.
When $Z_\cap>0$, every complementary pair contributes its unchanged
weight to $\exp(\Phi(\bm{y}))$. Writing
$M\coloneqq \max_S\mu(S)\max_T\nu(T)$, we therefore have
\begin{align*}
 \Phi(\bm{y})&\ge\log Z_\cap\ge\log\frac{M}{{\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu},&
 \Phi(\bm{0})&\le\log(4^nM).
\end{align*}
Thus the required gap bound is at most $B$, so take $H_0\coloneqq B$;
no minimizing point need exist.

Take $\delta=1/64$ in \cref{thm:stochastic-coordinate-descent}.
The algorithm uses at most $Q_{\mathrm{cd}}=O(n^4B\log(2B))$ gradient
samples and $O(T'Q_{\mathrm{cd}})$ operations, where $T'$ bounds the
cost of one gradient sample. It also gives
$\|\bm{y}\|_1=O(B/\eta+\eta)=O(nB)$ for every queried or returned point,
which proves \cref{eq:balancing-bounds}.
We stop and report failure before exceeding any of these bounds.
Thus they also hold when $Z_\cap=0$; when $Z_\cap>0$, this stopping
rule does not change the algorithm with exact samples.

Supply each gradient sample using \cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling},
with fresh randomness and total variation error at most
$1/(64Q_{\mathrm{cd}})$.
By \cref{rem:approximate-sampling}, these sampling errors add at most
$1/64$ to the failure probability. Hence the algorithm finds the
required field with probability at least $1-1/64-1/64=31/32$
when $Z_\cap>0$.

For the running time, the field bound gives
$n\log(z_{\max}/z_{\min})=O(n^2B)$ at every query.
Since $t^{-1}=256 n^2$ and $B=\Theta(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))$,
\cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling} gives $T'=O(n^6B)$ operations and
value-oracle calls per gradient sample.
Multiplying by $Q_{\mathrm{cd}}$ proves the claimed bound;
the $O(nQ_{\mathrm{cd}})$ additional operations cost less.
The field updates can be implemented using arithmetic operations only;
see \cref{app:counting-arithmetic}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The cases $a=0$ or $b=0$ are evaluated directly, so assume $n\ge2$.
We choose fields making complementary pairs frequent, then estimate
the two unknown factors in
\begin{align}\label{eq:counting-factorization}
 Z_\cap&=\frac{Z_{t,\bm{z}}}{\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}} \times
          \pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S).
\end{align}
Let $B,t$ be as in \cref{cor:balanced-fields}, and put
$\beta\coloneqq \varepsilon/4$ and $\delta_0\coloneqq 1/64$.
Apply \cref{cor:balanced-fields}; if it reports failure, return zero.
Otherwise fix the returned field $\bm{z}$. When $Z_\cap>0$, with probability
at least $1-2\delta_0$, this field satisfies
$\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\ge1/2$.

\paragraph{Estimating the normalizer.}
For any returned field $\bm{z}$, we apply
\cref{lem:sampling-to-counting} to the $2n$ membership bits of $(S,T)$,
with weight
\begin{align*}
 W(S,T)&\coloneqq \mu(S)\nu(T)t^{|S\cap T|}\bm{z}^S\bm{z}^T.
\end{align*}
The supplied pair $(S_0,T_0)$ is a valid starting state.

Each conditional law is obtained by restricting $\mu,\nu$ to the
prescribed inclusions and exclusions, with the same $t,\bm{z}$.
We keep the original ground set and the forced elements in each set,
so the degrees remain $a,b$. Inclusion replaces a generating polynomial
by its coordinate derivative times that variable; exclusion sets the
variable to zero. These operations preserve log-concavity, and the
coefficient ranges do not increase. For every nonempty
conditional law, both measures are nonzero. Thus \cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling} applies
to every conditional law.

\Cref{lem:sampling-to-counting}, with relative error
$\beta$ and failure probability $\delta_0$, therefore gives an estimate
$\widehat Z$ of $Z_{t,\bm{z}}$ using
$O(n^3\beta^{-2}\log(2n/\delta_0))$ conditional samples, each within
total variation distance $\beta/(32n)$ of its law.
The sample counts and running times are bounded on every execution.

\paragraph{Combining the estimates.}
Independently draw
$m=\lceil8\beta^{-2}\log(2/\delta_0)\rceil$ pairs from $\pi_{t,\bm{z}}$,
each to total variation error $\beta/4$, and let $\widehat p$ be the
fraction that are complementary. Conditional on the returned fields,
Hoeffding's inequality gives
$|\widehat p-\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)|\le\beta/2$ except with probability $\delta_0$:
the sampling bias is at most $\beta/4$, as is the fluctuation of
the empirical average. Return
\begin{align*}
 \widehat Z_\cap&\coloneqq \widehat p\,\widehat Z/\bm{z}^{{\mathcal{U}}}.
\end{align*}
{When the returned field satisfies
$\pi_{t,\bm{z}}(T={\mathcal{U}}\setminus S)\ge1/2$ and both preceding
estimation bounds hold, this is a product of two estimates, each with
relative error at most $\beta$. These conditions hold jointly with
probability at least $1-4\delta_0>3/4$, so}
\begin{align*}
 (1-\beta)^2&\le\widehat Z_\cap/Z_\cap\le(1+\beta)^2,
\end{align*}
which implies relative error $\varepsilon$. If $Z_\cap=0$, every supported
pair fails the complementary-pair test. Thus every execution returns
zero, either at the field-finding step or because $\widehat p=0$.

\paragraph{Running time.}
Finding the field costs $O(n^{10}B^2\log(2B))$ by
\cref{cor:balanced-fields}. Throughout the self-reduction, the
coefficient ranges do not increase, and
$n\log(z_{\max}/z_{\min})=O(n^2B)$ by
\cref{eq:balancing-bounds}. Each restricted oracle uses one original
query and $O(n)$ operations to check the prescribed memberships.
Thus \cref{cor:bases-pair-sampling}, with $t^{-1}= 256 n^2$, bounds the
cost of a conditional sample by
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^5\left(n^2B+\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)\right).
\end{align*}
Self-reduction uses $O(n^3\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2n))$ such samples.
Estimating the complementary-pair probability takes
$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ additional samples and is covered by the same bound.
Since $B=\Theta(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))$, the total cost is
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^{10}B^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2\frac{2B}{\varepsilon}\right),
\end{align*}
as required by \cref{eq:main-cost}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:positive-curvature-support}
Let $\omega$ be a nonzero nonnegative measure on $2^{{\mathcal{U}}}$ whose support
$\Omega$ is connected under single-element additions and deletions, and put
$V\coloneqq\bigcup_{S\in\Omega}S$.
If $\omega$ has upward spectral curvature \mbox{$\kappa>0$}, then $\Omega$ is upward closed in $2^V$.
In particular, if $\Omega$ is also downward closed, then $\Omega=2^V$,
where \mbox{$V=\{u:\omega(\{u\})>0\}$}.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:lc-support-access}
Let $g_\omega(\bm{x})=\sum_{A\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}}\omega(A)\bm{x}^A$ be nonzero and
log-concave, with nonnegative coefficients, and put $n\coloneqq |{\mathcal{U}}|$.
Given a value oracle for $\omega$, a set $A_0\in\operatorname{supp}\omega$, and disjoint
$C,O\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}$, an algorithm using $O(n^3)$ queries can:
\begin{itemize}
\item certify that no $A\in\operatorname{supp}\omega$ contains $C$ and avoids $O$; or
\item find, for every size at which such a set exists, a set
$A\in\operatorname{supp}\omega$ containing $C$ and avoiding $O$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:lc-homogeneous-layers}
Let $g$ be a multiaffine log-concave polynomial with nonnegative
coefficients. For each degree $k$, the sum of the degree-$k$ terms of $g$
is either zero or log-concave.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
By the reduction above, it suffices to estimate $Z_\cap$,
using \cref{thm:homogeneous-convolution}, proved in \cref{sec:fpras}.
Write $g_{\mu,k}$ for the sum of the degree-$k$ terms of $g_\mu$,
and similarly for $\nu$. By \cref{lem:lc-homogeneous-layers}, each of
these polynomials is either zero or log-concave. Then
\begin{align*}
 Z_\cap&=\sum_{k=0}^n
     [\bm{x}^{\mathcal{U}}]\bigl(g_{\mu,k}(\bm{x})g_{\nu,n-k}(\bm{x})\bigr).
\end{align*}
Each layer inherits its value oracle and coefficient-range bound;
\cref{lem:lc-support-access} supplies {sets of positive weight} in all nonempty
layers using $O(n^3)$ queries. Apply \cref{thm:homogeneous-convolution}
to each pair of nonempty layers, with relative error $\varepsilon$ and failure
probability $1/(4(n+1))$, using $O(\log(2n))$ repetitions.
Summing the estimates and taking a union bound proves the guarantee.
{The at most $n+1$ applications of \cref{eq:main-cost}, including
the repetitions needed to boost the success probability, cost}
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^{11}(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))^2\varepsilon^{-2}
       \log(2n)\log^2\frac{2(n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu))}{\varepsilon}\right).
\end{align*}
This is the bound in \cref{thm:log-concave-convolution}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By the reduction above, it suffices to estimate $Z_\cap$.
If $\max\{\kappa,\eta\}=0$, then $\eta=\kappa=0$ and
\cref{prop:zero-curvature-log-concavity} makes both generating polynomials
log-concave; the empty sets supply {starting sets of positive weight}. Thus
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} applies, and its cost is the first term in the stated bound.
It remains to treat the case $\max\{\eta,\kappa\}>0$, whose cost is the
second term.

\paragraph{The case $\max\{\eta,\kappa\}>0$.}
Interchange $\mu$ and $\nu$ if necessary so that $\nu$ has upward
spectral curvature $\kappa=\gamma>0$.
Since $\operatorname{supp}\nu$ is downward closed and hence connected, the final conclusion of \cref{lem:positive-curvature-support} gives
$\operatorname{supp}\nu=2^V$, where $V\coloneqq \{u:\nu(\{u\})>0\}$.
As in the reduction above, we may assume without loss of generality
that $V={\mathcal{U}}$, by pinning ${\mathcal{U}}\setminus V$ into $\mu$
and restricting to $V$ (returning zero if the pinning is infeasible,
and evaluating the case $V=\varnothing$ directly).
The measure $\mu$ still has downward-closed support,
and $\operatorname{supp}\nu=2^{{\mathcal{U}}}$.

To obtain a positive gap even when $\eta+\kappa=0$, decrease the field
of $\mu$ by setting
\begin{align*}
 t&\coloneqq 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{16n},&
 \widetilde\mu(A)&\coloneqq t^{|A|}\mu(A).
\end{align*}
This multiplies each ratio $\mu(S+u)/\mu(S)$ by $t$ and each ratio
$\mu(S+u+v)/\mu(S)$, for distinct $u,v\notin S$, by $t^2$.
Substituting into \cref{def:spectral-curvature} with parameter
$t\eta$ gives
\[
 A_S^{\widetilde\mu,t\eta}=t^2A_S^{\mu,\eta}\succeq0.
\]
Thus $\widetilde\mu$ has upward spectral curvature $t\eta$, and
\[
 \delta\coloneqq t\eta+\kappa
 =t(\eta+\kappa)+(1-t)\kappa
 \ge\frac{\varepsilon\gamma}{16n}.
\]
Let $\widetilde Z_\cap$ be the convolution value with $\mu$ replaced by
$\widetilde\mu$. Since $t^n\ge1-\varepsilon/16$,
\[
 (1-\varepsilon/16)Z_\cap\le t^n Z_\cap\le\widetilde Z_\cap\le Z_\cap.
\]
{Thus an estimate of $\widetilde Z_\cap$ with relative error
at most $\varepsilon/4$ also estimates $Z_\cap$ with \mbox{relative error at most $\varepsilon$}.}

Apply \cref{thm:poincare} with first factor $\widetilde\mu$ and second
factor $\nu^*(A)=\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)$, restricted to
$\Omega\coloneqq \operatorname{supp}\mu$. The second factor needs downward curvature
$\kappa$, which follows from
\[
 D_A^{\nu^*,\kappa}=A_{{\mathcal{U}}\setminus A}^{\nu,\kappa}\succeq0.
\]
Restricting $\nu^*$ to $\Omega$ leaves these matrices unchanged,
since every deletion of a set in $\Omega$ remains in $\Omega$.
The resulting chain samples
$\rho(A)\propto\widetilde\mu(A)\nu^*(A)$, has gap at least $\delta$,
and has rates
\begin{align*}
 q(A,A+u)&=t\frac{\mu(A+u)}{\mu(A)},&
 q(A,A-u)&=\frac{\nu(({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)+u)}
                         {\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)}.
\end{align*}
Only the addition rates are multiplied by $t<1$.
Both rates are at most $B\coloneqq \chi\gamma$. Normalizing the rates by $2nB$
gives a lazy chain with gap at least
\[
 \frac{\delta}{2nB}
 \ge\frac{\varepsilon\gamma/(16n)}{2n\chi\gamma}
 =\frac{\varepsilon}{32\chi n^2}.
\]
The factor $\gamma$ cancels because the rate bound also contains $\gamma$.
The minimum stationary mass is at least $t^n/(2^n{\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)$,
and each step costs $O(1)$.
It starts from the supported empty set. The mixing bound
\cref{eq:poincare-mixing} gives a sample with total-variation
error $\tau$ in
\begin{align*}
 O\left(\frac{n^2\chi}{\varepsilon}
       \left[n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)+\log(1/\tau)\right]\right)
\end{align*}
steps. {The same bounds hold for the conditional distributions
obtained by fixing coordinates.}

\Cref{lem:sampling-to-counting}, applied to the $n$
membership bits with weight $\widetilde\mu(A)\nu({\mathcal{U}}\setminus A)$
and starting state $\varnothing$, estimates $\widetilde Z_\cap$ to
relative error $\varepsilon/4$, with success probability at least $3/4$, using
$O(n^3\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2n))$ conditional samples of accuracy
$\tau=\varepsilon/(64n)$. With fixed walk lengths, this gives total cost
\begin{align*}
 O\left(n^5\chi\varepsilon^{-3}\log(2n)
       \left[n+\log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)+\log\frac{2n}{\varepsilon}\right]\right)
\end{align*}
arithmetic operations and value-oracle calls on every execution.
The tilt bound gives the required relative estimate of $Z_\cap$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Fix $u\in V$. We show that $u$ can be added to every supported set
that does not already contain it. The key observation is that, along
an edge between two such sets, $u$ can be added at both endpoints or
at neither.

To see this, let $S,S+v\in\Omega$ with distinct $u,v\notin S$, and put
\[
 a=\frac{\omega(S+u)}{\omega(S)},\qquad
 b=\frac{\omega(S+v)}{\omega(S)}>0,\qquad
 c=\frac{\omega(S+u+v)}{\omega(S)}.
\]
The principal submatrix of $A_S^{\omega,\kappa}$ on $u,v$ is
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}a^2-\kappa a&ab-c\\ab-c&b^2-\kappa b\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
If $a=0$, the first diagonal entry is zero, so positive semidefiniteness
forces the off-diagonal entry to vanish, giving $c=0$.
If $a>0$, positive semidefiniteness also gives
\[
 0\le (b,-a)M(b,-a)^{\mathsf T}
 =ab\bigl(2c-\kappa(a+b)\bigr),
\]
so $c\ge\kappa(a+b)/2>0$.
Thus $a>0$ if and only if $c>0$, proving the observation.

Now take any $S\in\Omega$ with $u\notin S$.
Since $u\in V$ and $\Omega$ is connected, there is a path in $\Omega$
from $S$ to a set containing $u$. Stop at the first such set.
The last step adds $u$, so $u$ can be added to the preceding set.
Every earlier edge has both endpoints omitting $u$; by the observation,
working backwards along the path shows that $u$ can also be added to $S$.
Since $u\in V$ was arbitrary, $\Omega$ is upward closed in $2^V$.

If $\Omega$ is also downward closed, then $\varnothing\in\Omega$.
Upward closure now gives $\Omega=2^V$, and {the description of $V$
as the set of elements $u$ with $\omega(\{u\})>0$ follows}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $P\coloneqq \operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_A:A\in\operatorname{supp}\omega\}$, where
$\mathbf1_A$ is the incidence vector of $A$. This convex hull is the
\emph{Newton polytope} of $g_\omega$. Its vertices are precisely the
incidence vectors of sets in $\operatorname{supp}\omega$, and an \emph{edge} is a
one-dimensional face. By \cite[Proposition~10.4]{OveisGharan2020Lecture10},
every edge is parallel to a coordinate vector $\bm{e}_i$ or a difference
$\bm{e}_i-\bm{e}_j$. Consequently, a linear objective with no improving addition,
deletion, or exchange within $\operatorname{supp}\omega$ is globally optimal: these
moves include every incident edge. Starting at $A_0$, minimize
$|C\setminus A|+|A\cap O|$ by such moves. At most $n$ improvements,
each found with $O(n^2)$ queries, either produce a feasible set or
certify infeasibility. The convex hull of the feasible incidence vectors
is a face of $P$ and inherits its edge directions. Greedy additions and deletions
within this face therefore reach the maximum and minimum
cardinalities, visiting every intervening size in $O(n^2)$ further queries.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
We reduce counting proper two-colourings of a $3$-uniform hypergraph
to subset convolution. Deciding whether such a colouring exists is
$\mathsf{NP}$-complete~\cite{DinurRegevSmyth2005}.
Fix $\delta>0$ and a rational constant
$0<c<\min\{1,\delta/2\}$. For a $3$-uniform hypergraph
$\mathcal H=({\mathcal{U}},\mathcal F)$ with $n\coloneqq|{\mathcal{U}}|\ge1$, put
$a\coloneqq c/n$ and define
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal I&\coloneqq
 \{S\subseteq{\mathcal{U}}:F\nsubseteq S\text{ for every }F\in\mathcal F\},\\
 \mu(S)=\nu(S)&\coloneqq a^{|S|}\mathbf{1}[S\in\mathcal I].
\end{align*}
The two colour classes form a proper colouring exactly when both
belong to $\mathcal I$. Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 [\bm{x}^{{\mathcal{U}}}]\bigl(g_\mu(\bm{x})g_\nu(\bm{x})\bigr)
 &=a^n\,\#\{\text{proper two-colourings of }\mathcal H\}.
\end{align*}
Since $a^n$ is known, it remains to verify the promised curvature and
oracle bounds.

Fix $S\in\mathcal I$, and let
$J_S\coloneqq\{u\in{\mathcal{U}}\setminus S:S+u\in\mathcal I\}$ be its
feasible additions. On $J_S$, define the symmetric matrix
\begin{align*}
 B_S(u,v)&\coloneqq
 \mathbf{1}[u\ne v,\ S+u+v\notin\mathcal I].
\end{align*}
Each row of $B_S$ has at most $n-1$ nonzero entries, all equal to one,
so $B_S\succeq-(n-1)I$. Substituting the weight ratios into
\cref{def:spectral-curvature} gives
\begin{align*}
 A_S^{\mu,-c}\big|_{J_S\times J_S}
 &=a^2(I+B_S)+caI
 =a^2\bigl((n+1)I+B_S\bigr)
 \succeq2a^2I.
\end{align*}
All other rows and columns vanish by downward closure. Thus both
measures have upward curvature $-c$, and we may take
$\eta=\kappa=-c$, giving $\eta+\kappa=-2c>-\delta$.
Their common support is downward closed, their rational weights
are computable in polynomial time, and
\begin{align*}
 \log({\mathcal{R}}_\mu{\mathcal{R}}_\nu)&\le2n\log(1/a)
 =2n\log(n/c)=O(n\log n).
\end{align*}

An $\mathsf{FPRAS}$ on these instances would therefore give a
bounded-error polynomial-time test for hypergraph two-colourability.
By reducing the decision queries in the usual $\mathsf{SAT}$
self-reduction to this problem, amplifying their success probabilities,
and verifying the resulting assignment, we obtain an $\mathsf{RP}$
algorithm for $\mathsf{SAT}$. Hence $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
We average the noisy gradients and take a fixed step in any coordinate
whose empirical derivative is large. Choose
\begin{align}
 \frac{\eta}{16L}&\le s\le\frac{\eta}{8L},\label{eq:scd-step}\\
 K&\coloneqq \lceil128LH_0\eta^{-2}\rceil+1,\qquad
 m_b\coloneqq \left\lceil32\sigma^2\eta^{-2}
 \log\bigl(2d(K+1)/\delta\bigr)\right\rceil.\label{eq:balance-params}
\end{align}
Start at $\bm{x}\coloneqq \bm{x}_0$. At each iteration, average $m_b$ fresh oracle
vectors to obtain $\widehat{\bm{g}}\coloneqq m_b^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m_b}\bm{G}^{(j)}(\bm{x})$.
Return $\bm{x}$ if $\|\widehat{\bm{g}}\|_\infty\le\eta/2$; otherwise declare
failure if $K$ updates have already occurred, and otherwise choose
$i$ with $|\widehat g_i|>\eta/2$ and update
\begin{align*}
 \bm{x}&\leftarrow \bm{x}-s\operatorname{sign}(\widehat g_i)\bm{e}_i,
 \qquad \operatorname{sign}(u)\coloneqq u/|u|\quad(u\ne0).
\end{align*}
There are at most $K+1$ batches and $K$ updates, so every queried or
returned point is $\bm{x}=\bm{x}_0+s\bm{k}$ for an integer vector $\bm{k}$ satisfying
\begin{align}\label{eq:scd-field-bound}
 \|\bm{k}\|_1&\le K,\qquad
 \|\bm{x}-\bm{x}_0\|_1\le Ks\le16H_0/\eta+\eta/(4L).
\end{align}
These deterministic bounds give \cref{eq:scd-iterates}. Moreover,
$(K+1)m_b=O(Q)$ for $Q$ in \cref{eq:scd-budget}; averaging and
selecting a coordinate cost $O(dm_b)$ per batch, so $T\ge d$ gives
the total cost $O(TQ)$ on every history.

For correctness, conditional sub-Gaussian concentration gives
\begin{align*}
  \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbf{Pr}\left[|\widehat g_i-\partial_i f(\bm{x})|>\eta/4\mid\text{past}\right]}
  {\mathbf{Pr}_{}\left[|\widehat g_i-\partial_i f(\bm{x})|>\eta/4\mid\text{past}\right]} 
 &\le2\mathrm{e}^{-m_b\eta^2/(32\sigma^2)}
 \le\frac{\delta}{d(K+1)}.
\end{align*}
Thus, with probability at least $1-\delta$, every coordinate estimate
in every batch is accurate within $\eta/4$. On this event, any returned
point satisfies $\|\nabla f(\bm{x})\|_\infty\le3\eta/4<\eta$.
Each updated coordinate has $|\partial_i f(\bm{x})|>\eta/4$ and the same
sign $\tau\coloneqq \operatorname{sign}(\widehat g_i)$ as its estimate. By
\cref{eq:coordinate-smoothness} and \cref{eq:scd-step},
\begin{align}
 f(\bm{x}-s\tau\bm{e}_i)
 &\le f(\bm{x})-s|\partial_i f(\bm{x})|+Ls^2/2\notag\\
 &\le f(\bm{x})-\frac{\eta^2}{64L}+\frac{\eta^2}{128L}
 =f(\bm{x})-\frac{\eta^2}{128L}.\label{eq:descent}
\end{align}
After $K$ updates this would give
$f(\bm{x})\le f(\bm{x}_0)-K\eta^2/(128L)<f(\bm{x}_0)-H_0$, contradicting
the lower bound. Hence the algorithm returns before making $K$ updates.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:bit-complexity}
For rational input parameters and polynomial-time value oracles returning
rationals of polynomial encoding length, the algorithm in
\cref{thm:log-concave-convolution} has an implementation whose running time
is polynomial in the input length and $\varepsilon^{-1}$ on every execution.
Indeed, the update rule above gives $z_u=(1+1/(32n))^{k_u}$ for integers
$k_u$, and the field bound \cref{eq:balancing-bounds} implies
$\sum_u|k_u|=O(n^2B)$. Each field coordinate can therefore be stored using
polynomially many bits. The probabilities for choosing which element
to add back are ratios of sums of at most $n$ weighted oracle values,
and empirical frequencies are
ratios of sample counts. The final estimate uses products and ratios
of these numbers, fields, and powers of $t$. All these numbers have
polynomially many bits.

{We simulate the required rational probabilities using fair coin flips;
see \cite[Proposition~13]{NacuPeres2005}.}
Each binary choice can be simulated with probability at most $2^{-r}$
of requiring more than $r$ bits. If $N$ is a polynomial bound on the
total number of binary choices in the homogeneous algorithm, aborting
and returning zero when any choice needs more than
$\lceil\log_2(64N)\rceil$ bits adds at most $1/64$ to its failure
probability. The success probability proved in \cref{sec:fpras} is at
least $15/16$, so it remains above $3/4$. Conditioning, amplification,
and summation over homogeneous layers preserve polynomial bit complexity.
In particular, the rational
six-vertex instances in \cref{app:quantum} satisfy these oracle assumptions.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Expanding $p(\mathbf1+\bm{x})$ using its nonnegative coefficients shows
that $\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu$ is downward closed.
For $S\in\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu$, set $q\coloneqq \partial_Sp$, so
$q(\mathbf1)=\widehat\mu(S)>0$.
As verified below, $q$ is $\alpha$-fractionally log-concave.
The coefficient ratios in \cref{def:spectral-curvature} and the
chain rule therefore give
\begin{align*}
 A_S^{\widehat\mu,\,1-\alpha^{-1}}
 &=-\nabla^2\log q(\mathbf1)
   -(1-\alpha^{-1})\operatorname{diag}(\nabla\log q(\mathbf1))\\
 &=-\alpha^{-2}
   \left.\nabla_{\bm{x}}^2\log q(x_1^\alpha,\ldots,x_n^\alpha)
   \right|_{\bm{x}=\mathbf1}\succeq0,
\end{align*}
which proves the asserted curvature bound.

It remains to verify that nonzero coordinate derivatives preserve
fractional log-concavity. We use the limiting argument of
\cite[Section~1.5]{AlimohammadiAnariShiragurVuong2021}.
Writing $\bm{x}^\alpha\coloneqq (x_1^\alpha,\ldots,x_n^\alpha)$, multiaffinity gives
\begin{align*}
 (\partial_i p)(\bm{x}^\alpha)
 &=\lim_{s\to\infty}s^{-\alpha}p\bigl((\bm{x}+s\bm{e}_i)^\alpha\bigr).
\end{align*}
Each function on the right is a positive multiple of a translate
of $\bm{x}\mapsto p(\bm{x}^\alpha)$, hence is log-concave. The log-concavity
inequality is preserved under the limit. Iterating proves the assertion
for every nonzero $\partial_Sp$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Reversing paths whose intermediate states lie outside $B$ and applying
detailed balance gives $\pi(x)r^B(x,y)=\pi(y)r^B(y,x)$, proving
reversibility with respect to $\pi_B$.
To transfer the Poincar\'e inequality, extend $f:B\to\mathbb R$
to $\Omega$ by
\[
 h(x)\coloneqq \ifthenelse{\isempty{}}
  {\mathbb{E}\left[f(X_{\tau_B})\mid X_0=x\right]}
  {\mathbb{E}_{}\left[f(X_{\tau_B})\mid X_0=x\right]} .
\]
Then $h=f$ on $B$. We claim that
\[
 ({\mathcal{L}}_rh)(x)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&x\notin B,\\
  ({\mathcal{L}}_{r^B}f)(x),&x\in B.
 \end{cases}
\]
Assuming these identities, we have
${\mathcal{E}}_r(h,h)=\pi(B){\mathcal{E}}_{r^B}(f,f)$, while the law of total variance
gives $ \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[h\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[h\right]} \ge\pi(B) \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi_B}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_B}\left[f\right]} $. Applying the original
Poincar\'e inequality yields
\begin{align*}
 \pi(B){\mathcal{E}}_{r^B}(f,f)
 &={\mathcal{E}}_r(h,h)\\
 &\ge\gamma \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[h\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi}\left[h\right]} 
 \ge\gamma\pi(B) \ifthenelse{\isempty{\pi_B}}
{\mathbf{Var}\left[f\right]}
{\mathbf{Var}_{\pi_B}\left[f\right]} .
\end{align*}
Canceling $\pi(B)>0$ proves the desired inequality.

It remains to verify the two identities. For $x\notin B$, expanding
the definition gives
\begin{align*}
 ({\mathcal{L}}_rh)(x)
 &=\sum_{y\ne x}r(x,y)(h(x)-h(y))\\
 &=\left(\sum_{y\ne x}r(x,y)\right)h(x)
   -\sum_{y\ne x}r(x,y)h(y)=0,
\end{align*}
where the last equality is justified as follows. Put
$q_x\coloneqq\sum_{z\ne x}r(x,z)>0$, and let
$\tau\coloneqq\inf\{s>0:X_s\ne X_0\}$ be the first jump time.
Starting from $x$, the first jump goes to $y\ne x$ with probability
$r(x,y)/q_x$. Since $x\notin B$, the chain has not hit $B$ before
